option1: The client class keeps growing and must be edited every time a new shape is added — object-creation logic is scattered wherever objects are needed
option2: Circle and Square would need to implement the same interface, which Java doesn't allow
option3: It would cause a compile-time ambiguous-method error
option4: The new keyword can only be called a limited number of times per class
correctOptionExplanation: Scattering `new` calls across the codebase means every new type requires hunting down every call site — centralizing this is the first motivation for a factory.

option1: It eliminates the new keyword from the codebase entirely
option2: It centralizes creation logic in one place (fixes scattering), but still has an if-else chain that must be edited for every new shape (doesn't fix OCP)
option3: It fixes OCP completely — no class ever needs editing again to add a new shape
option4: It removes the need for Circle/Square/Rectangle to implement a common interface
correctOptionExplanation: Centralization and OCP-compliance are two separate wins — Simple Factory only gives you the first one.

questionText: The course notes explicitly state Simple Factory "is not really a design pattern" and "breaks OCP." Why does it break OCP specifically?
option1: It doesn't actually break OCP — the notes are describing Factory Method instead
option2: It breaks OCP because choice is passed as an int instead of an enum
option3: Every time a new shape type is added, ShapeFactory.getShape()'s existing if-else body must be modified — the class is not closed for modification
option4: It breaks OCP because Shape must be an interface, not a class
correctOptionExplanation: OCP requires being open for extension but closed for modification; every new shape forces you to reopen and edit getShape()'s body.

option1: It removes the need for a choice parameter entirely
option2: It completely solves OCP with zero remaining limitations
option3: It makes Shape unnecessary since the map handles typing
option4: getObj() itself never needs editing again (no more if-else branches to add) — but the map still has to be populated with a new entry per type somewhere, and it's now hardcoded to a fixed, non-changing set decided upfront
correctOptionExplanation: The branching moves from inside getObj() to the map's population step — an improvement, but a new type still requires editing the setup code somewhere.

questionText: In the hashmap version, map.get(choice) returns the SAME pre-constructed object instance every time getObj(1) is called. What behavior does this cause that a fresh new Circle() per call wouldn't?
option1: Every caller of getObj(1) receives a reference to one shared Circle instance — mutating it in one place would be visible everywhere it's used
option2: getObj() becomes unusable after the first call since the map entry is consumed
option3: It automatically creates a new Circle each time under the hood, identical to new Circle()
option4: It throws a ConcurrentModificationException on the second call
correctOptionExplanation: HashMap.get() just returns the stored reference — it doesn't construct anything new, so shared mutable state becomes a real risk.

questionText: Given the hashmap-based factory returns shared pre-built instances, in what kind of real scenario would this actually be the RIGHT choice rather than a limitation?
option1: Only in single-threaded programs
option2: When the objects being returned are stateless or meant to be shared/reused (similar to why PlayState/PauseState/StopState in class-20 were made Singletons) — no per-use uniqueness is needed
option3: Never — sharing instances is always a bug regardless of context
option4: Only when choice is a String instead of an int
correctOptionExplanation: This connects directly back to class-20's insight: stateless objects are safe (and often preferable) to share as single instances.

questionText: If you wanted the hashmap factory to return a brand-new object each time instead of a shared one, what would you have to change?
option1: Change Map<Integer, Shape> to Map<Integer, Integer>
option2: Mark the map as volatile
option3: Store a way to construct new instances (e.g. a Supplier<Shape> or constructor reference per key) instead of storing already-built objects, and call it fresh inside getObj()
option4: Nothing — HashMap.get() already constructs a new object automatically for non-primitive types
correctOptionExplanation: You'd need the map to hold factories/suppliers of shapes rather than the shapes themselves, so each get() triggers fresh construction.

questionText: A teammate says: "Simple Factory is basically the same thing as Factory Method, just written differently." Based on how the course structures these as separate concepts, what's the actual structural difference?
option1: They are functionally and structurally identical — the distinction is purely academic
option2: Simple Factory always returns interfaces, Factory Method always returns abstract classes
option3: Factory Method is Simple Factory with multithreading added
option4: Simple Factory is one class with an if-else/map branching internally on a passed-in choice; Factory Method has no branching at all — each subclass overrides an abstract creation method to return its own fixed type, with the choice of subclass made by which class you instantiate
correctOptionExplanation: Simple Factory branches at runtime inside one method; Factory Method resolves the branch at compile time via subclass selection — a fundamentally different mechanism.

questionText: If your app has 3 shape types today and you're confident that number will grow every few weeks as new shape types are added, why might the notes' framing suggest moving away from Simple Factory (map or if-else based) toward Factory Method or Abstract Factory instead?
option1: Both if-else and hashmap Simple Factory require editing the factory's own source (new branch, or new map entry) for every new type, while Factory Method lets you add a new type by writing an entirely new subclass without touching existing factory code at all
option2: Factory Method requires fewer total classes than Simple Factory in every case
option3: Simple Factory is objectively faster at runtime, so this tradeoff doesn't matter
option4: Simple Factory cannot return interface types, only concrete classes
correctOptionExplanation: Frequent growth is exactly the scenario where OCP violations (constant edits to existing code) become a real maintenance cost, motivating the move to Factory Method.

questionText: Given Map<Integer, Shape> map populated with 1 -> obj1, 2 -> obj2, 3 -> obj3 and getObj(choice) { return map.get(choice); }, what happens if getObj(4) is called and no entry exists for key 4?
option1: It automatically falls back to obj1
option2: It returns null — HashMap.get() on a missing key returns null rather than throwing, so the caller must handle a possible null result
option3: It throws a NoSuchElementException
option4: It throws a compile-time error since 4 wasn't declared as a valid choice
correctOptionExplanation: HashMap.get() never throws for a missing key — it silently returns null, a common source of downstream NullPointerExceptions if not checked.

option1: IEnemy itself contains a static factory method that all Level subclasses call
option2: It lives inside Level.startLevel() directly via an if-else on level type
option3: It lives inside ForestLevel.createEnemy() — startLevel() only calls the abstract createEnemy() and works polymorphically, staying identical regardless of which subclass runs it
option4: Main.java constructs the Goblin and passes it into startLevel() as a parameter
correctOptionExplanation: startLevel() is a fixed skeleton that delegates the varying part (which enemy) to whichever subclass is actually running.

option1: It throws a ClassCastException since the variable name doesn't match the object type
option2: Nothing — Level requires the variable name to match the subclass name to compile
option3: A Goblin — since the variable is named forest, matching ForestLevel
option4: A SnowMan — the variable name is irrelevant; the actual object is SnowLevel, whose createEnemy() returns new SnowMan(), so startLevel() calls SnowMan.attack()
correctOptionExplanation: Variable names are purely for the programmer's benefit — Java dispatches based on the actual runtime object type, not the identifier used to reference it.

questionText: createEnemy() in Level.java has no access modifier (package-private), and ForestLevel/SnowLevel/DesertLevel override it also without an access modifier. What would happen if createEnemy() were instead declared private abstract IEnemy createEnemy();?
option1: It wouldn't compile — private and abstract are contradictory; a private method can't be overridden, but abstract methods must be overridable by definition
option2: It would silently become a static method instead
option3: startLevel() would need to be made private too
option4: It would compile fine and work identically, just with stricter encapsulation
correctOptionExplanation: private hides a method from subclasses entirely, while abstract exists specifically to be implemented by subclasses — the two modifiers cannot coexist.

questionText: If you want to add a CaveLevel that spawns a new Bat implements IEnemy, what exactly must you touch in the existing Level, ForestLevel, SnowLevel, and DesertLevel classes?
option1: You must edit IEnemy to add a isCaveEnemy() method
option2: Nothing in any of them — you write Bat implements IEnemy and CaveLevel extends Level with its own createEnemy() override, and the existing classes remain completely untouched
option3: You must add a new branch inside Level.startLevel() to handle the Cave case
option4: You must edit ForestLevel since it's the first subclass and acts as a base for new ones
correctOptionExplanation: This is Factory Method's core OCP payoff: new variants are pure additions, never edits to existing code.

questionText: startLevel() is concrete (has a body) while createEnemy() is abstract, both living in the same Level class. What established course pattern is Level structurally combining with Factory Method here?
option1: Singleton — because Level has only one instance per subclass
option2: Adapter — because Level adapts IEnemy to a different interface
option3: Template Method — startLevel() is a fixed-skeleton method that calls a varying abstract step (createEnemy()), the same shape as BeverageMaker.makeBeverage() calling abstract brew()
option4: Observer — because startLevel() notifies enemies of level start
correctOptionExplanation: Factory Method is frequently found nested inside a Template Method's fixed skeleton, exactly as seen with BeverageMaker/PaymentProcessor earlier in the course.

questionText: If Goblin, SnowMan, and SandMan all had identical attack() bodies except for the printed string, would IEnemy still be worth having as an interface rather than just using one Enemy class with a type field and an if-else in attack()?
option1: IEnemy provides no benefit since attack() never varies polymorphically here
option2: No — with only one line different per enemy, a single class with a type field is strictly better in every case
option3: It only matters once there are more than 5 enemy types
option4: Yes — the interface keeps Level.createEnemy() and startLevel() decoupled from concrete enemy types entirely; the if-else version would need every attack() call site (or the class itself) to branch on type, reintroducing the exact problem Factory Method avoids
correctOptionExplanation: Even simple variation-by-string reintroduces if-else branching somewhere — keeping the interface preserves the pattern's benefit regardless of how small the difference between implementations is.

questionText: Compare Level's Factory Method (createEnemy(), one product per subclass) to the earlier Simple Factory (ShapeFactory.getShape(int choice), one class branching on a parameter). What's the fundamental structural difference in HOW the "which type to create" decision gets made?
option1: Simple Factory decides at runtime via a parameter checked inside one method's branching logic; Factory Method decides at compile/construction time via which subclass you instantiate — no branching logic exists anywhere
option2: Factory Method requires reflection to decide the type; Simple Factory doesn't
option3: They're identical — both decide the type via a runtime parameter
option4: Simple Factory can only create one object per program run; Factory Method can create unlimited objects
correctOptionExplanation: This is the crux of the two patterns' difference: parameter-driven branching versus subclass-driven polymorphism.

questionText: A tester wants to unit-test that ForestLevel.startLevel() calls Goblin.attack() specifically, without worrying about SnowLevel or DesertLevel at all. What does the Factory Method structure make easy here that a single LevelFactory.getEnemy(int levelType) (Simple-Factory style) wouldn't?
option1: Simple Factory style is actually easier to test since everything is in one method
option2: Each Level subclass is independently testable in isolation — testing ForestLevel never requires touching or even being aware of SnowLevel's or DesertLevel's code, unlike a single shared factory method holding all branches together
option3: Neither approach is testable without mocking IEnemy first
option4: Factory Method requires a separate test framework, unlike Simple Factory
correctOptionExplanation: Isolation of each variant into its own subclass is a natural testability win that falls out of Factory Method's structure.

questionText: If DesertLevel.createEnemy() were changed to sometimes return a SandMan and sometimes return a new Scorpion() based on a random roll, would this still be "Factory Method" in the pattern sense?
option1: Yes, but only if Scorpion and SandMan share a common parent class instead of both implementing IEnemy
option2: No — Factory Method requires each subclass to always return exactly one hardcoded type with no variation
option3: Yes — Factory Method only requires that subclasses control what gets created via the overridden method; the method's internal logic (fixed, random, conditional) is an implementation detail, not part of the pattern's definition
option4: No — introducing randomness converts it into the Strategy pattern automatically
correctOptionExplanation: The pattern's definition is about WHERE the creation decision lives (the overridden method), not about how deterministic that method's internal logic is.

questionText: IEnemy has exactly one method, attack(). If a new requirement demands enemies also have a getHealthPoints() method, what's required across Goblin, SnowMan, and SandMan, and does this have anything to do with Factory Method itself?
option1: Level.createEnemy() must be changed to call getHealthPoints() internally for this to work
option2: Only Goblin needs it, since it's the first enemy class created
option3: Factory Method automatically generates getHealthPoints() for all IEnemy implementers
option4: Each of the three concrete enemy classes must implement getHealthPoints() since it becomes part of the IEnemy contract — this is unrelated to Factory Method, which only governs how enemies get created, not what methods IEnemy itself declares
correctOptionExplanation: Growing the IEnemy interface itself is an ISP/interface-design concern, separate from how Factory Method governs the moment of object creation.

option1: FurnitureFactory produces a whole FAMILY of related products (a matching Chair + Sofa) through one factory object, whereas Level's Factory Method produces just one product type (an enemy) per subclass
option2: There's no real difference — both are Factory Method, just with different names
option3: FurnitureFactory is only usable with exactly two product types, by definition
option4: FurnitureFactory uses static methods while Level uses instance methods
correctOptionExplanation: Abstract Factory generalizes Factory Method from "one product" to "a coordinated family of products" created via a single factory object.

option1: Yes — FurnitureStore would need an explicit if check to prevent mixing, which is missing from the real code
option2: No — since both createChair() and createSofa() are called on the SAME factory instance, and that instance is fixed at construction, the family stays consistent by construction
option3: Yes — createChair() and createSofa() could independently resolve to different families since they're separate method calls
option4: Only if Chair and Sofa share a common parent interface
correctOptionExplanation: Because factory is a single fixed field, every product pulled from it necessarily belongs to the same family — this guarantee is Abstract Factory's whole point.

questionText: This "family consistency guarantee" — that you literally cannot end up with a mismatched Modern chair + Victorian sofa as long as you go through one factory — is Abstract Factory's core selling point over what alternative?
option1: Manually calling ShapeFactory.getShape(choice) for both chair and sofa
option2: Using Level.createEnemy() for both chair and sofa creation
option3: Manually calling new ModernChair() and new VictorianSofa() directly wherever furniture is needed, where nothing stops a typo or copy-paste error from mixing families
option4: There's no real alternative being contrasted — Abstract Factory is the only way to create two related objects
correctOptionExplanation: The contrast is against direct, uncoordinated `new` calls scattered through client code, where nothing enforces that related objects stay from the same family.

questionText: To add a third theme, ScandinavianFurnitureFactory, what exactly needs to be created, and does FurnitureStore.java need any changes?
option1: Chair and Sofa interfaces must each be extended with Scandinavian variants
option2: FurnitureStore.furnishRoom() must add a new else if branch for the Scandinavian case
option3: FurnitureFactory interface itself must be edited to add Scandinavian-specific methods
option4: Create ScandinavianChair implements Chair, ScandinavianSofa implements Sofa, and ScandinavianFurnitureFactory implements FurnitureFactory — FurnitureStore needs zero changes since it only depends on the FurnitureFactory interface
correctOptionExplanation: Adding a new family is a pure addition of new classes — the client (FurnitureStore) never needs modification.

questionText: If a new product type, Table, needs to be added to every existing furniture family (Modern gets a ModernTable, Victorian gets a VictorianTable), what DOES need to change now, unlike adding a new theme in the previous question?
option1: FurnitureFactory interface itself needs a new createTable() method, which forces every existing implementer (ModernFurnitureFactory, VictorianFurnitureFactory) to be edited to provide it — adding a new PRODUCT is expensive, unlike adding a new FAMILY
option2: Nothing changes anywhere — Abstract Factory handles new product types with zero edits, symmetric to new themes
option3: Only FurnitureStore needs editing, not the factories themselves
option4: Chair and Sofa interfaces need a shared parent interface before Table can be added
correctOptionExplanation: This is Abstract Factory's known asymmetry: cheap to extend with new families, expensive to extend with new product types across all families.

questionText: The previous two questions together reveal an asymmetry in Abstract Factory's extensibility. How would you summarize it in one sentence?
option1: Both adding a new family and adding a new product type are equally expensive in Abstract Factory
option2: Adding a new FAMILY (new factory + matching product set) is cheap and requires zero changes to existing code, but adding a new PRODUCT TYPE across all existing families is expensive since it forces every existing factory implementation to be edited
option3: Abstract Factory doesn't support adding new families at all, only new product types
option4: Both adding a new family and adding a new product type are equally cheap in Abstract Factory
correctOptionExplanation: This mirrors a very common real-world tradeoff: Abstract Factory optimizes for "more variants of the same shape," not for "changing the shape itself."

option1: FurnitureFactory as a parameter type is required because Java forbids concrete classes as constructor parameters
option2: It's purely stylistic — FurnitureStore would behave identically either way, with no design implication
option3: Main is the composition root deciding which concrete factory to use; typing the constructor parameter to the interface means FurnitureStore itself never needs to change to support a new theme — only Main needs a one-line change to switch families
option4: Main acts as the Abstract Factory itself, and ModernFurnitureFactory is just a data holder
correctOptionExplanation: Depending on the abstraction (FurnitureFactory) rather than a concrete class is the DIP payoff — the client's only coupling point to a specific theme lives in Main, not inside FurnitureStore.

questionText: Compare FurnitureFactory (Abstract Factory, createChair() + createSofa() together) to Level (Factory Method, just createEnemy()). If Level were extended to ALSO create a matching IWeapon per level (e.g. ForestLevel creates a Goblin + a themed Dagger, SnowLevel creates a SnowMan + a themed IceSpear), what would Level effectively be evolving into?
option1: This isn't possible in Java — one class can only have one abstract factory method
option2: It would just be a bigger Factory Method with two abstract methods, unrelated to Abstract Factory at all
option3: It would become Simple Factory instead, since two objects are now returned
option4: It would evolve from plain Factory Method into something structurally like Abstract Factory — producing a matched FAMILY (enemy + weapon) per level/theme, rather than just one product
correctOptionExplanation: This is exactly the natural growth path from Factory Method to Abstract Factory: once you need more than one coordinated product per variant, you're building a family, which is Abstract Factory's territory.

questionText: Chair and Sofa are separate, unrelated interfaces (sitOn() vs lieOn()) — FurnitureFactory just happens to know how to create one of each. Is it a requirement of Abstract Factory that all products in a family share a common parent interface?
option1: No — Abstract Factory only requires that the FACTORY interface declares one creation method per product type in the family; the products themselves (Chair, Sofa) can be entirely unrelated types, as shown here
option2: Yes — Chair and Sofa would need to both implement a shared Furniture interface for this to be valid Abstract Factory
option3: No, but only if there are fewer than 3 products per family
option4: Yes — otherwise FurnitureStore.furnishRoom() wouldn't compile
correctOptionExplanation: Abstract Factory coordinates creation of a family, but does not require the family members themselves to share an interface — Chair and Sofa here are proof of that.

questionText: A junior dev asks: "Why not just skip Abstract Factory and have FurnitureStore call new ModernChair() and new ModernSofa() directly, with an if(theme.equals("modern")) check inside furnishRoom()?" Using everything covered across Simple Factory, Factory Method, and Abstract Factory, what's the most complete answer?
option1: The if-else version is actually preferable since it avoids creating extra factory classes
option2: That reintroduces the exact if-else-branching-on-type problem Simple Factory already showed is fragile and breaks OCP — every new theme means editing furnishRoom() directly, whereas the real Abstract Factory design lets FurnitureStore stay untouched and only requires a new factory class per theme, consistent with the Factory Method and Abstract Factory principles already established
option3: This concern only applies to Simple Factory, not to Abstract Factory-style code
option4: There's no real downside — both approaches are equally maintainable regardless of how many themes exist
correctOptionExplanation: This question ties the whole 30-question arc together: the if-else problem shown in Simple Factory never actually goes away on its own — Factory Method and Abstract Factory are the deliberate structural fixes for it.
